question.text: Saksham Skills Pvt Ltd (Section 8 FPE on BSE-SSE, skills training) earns (a) INR 1.2 cr from government-funded skilling of rural youth (covered by exemption notification) and (b) INR 60 lakh from corporate training-consultancy to private firms (fee-for-service). How should the SIA describe the GST treatment in the financial-compliance annexure to the Annual Impact Report?

answer.text: Both streams are GST-exempt because the entity is a Section 8 company
Both streams are taxable at 18% because GST makes no distinction for SSE-listed entities
The government-funded skilling is exempt under specific notification; the corporate consultancy stream is taxable at 18% GST (fee-for-service)
Both streams are taxable at 5% concessional GST for Section 8 FPEs on SSE

explanation.text: The Logic: GST law exempts specified social-sector services — notably charitable healthcare and education/skilling covered by notified government programmes. However, purely fee-for-service engagements (corporate training, advisory/consultancy, commercial health packages) are taxable at the standard 18% rate. The SE must therefore maintain separate books for exempt vs taxable revenue and restrict input tax credit to the taxable stream — a frequent SIA reconciliation point. The Trap: Section 8 status is a Companies Act concept and does NOT confer GST exemption. There is no blanket 5% or 18% concession 'for SSE-listed entities'. Eligibility is activity-based via notifications. Cross-Exam Context: XII (Securities Markets Foundation) and V-A touch indirect-tax basics. XXIII frames the question at the output-mix level that affects impact-per-rupee calculations. Assessor's Pro-Tip: When computing cost-per-beneficiary for SAS-200/SAS-1100 skills engagements, strip out GST from fee-for-service lines (since that is a tax pass-through, not programme spend). Including gross GST inflates the cost base and distorts SROI comparisons with pure charitable peers.
